doc.title: Rusty Dedrick interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Town bands and the Depression
summary: Town band concerts as social fabric and the Depression's limited effect on a farm family.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: So your family was, when you said playing in a country band—
A town band, okay, so you’re playing the Sousa and the marches and the summer concerts.
They’re still around, but that was a big part of the community in those days wasn’t it?
Oh yes. On the scene at the time, part of the social fabric of it. It was great.
Was your family affected at all by the depression?
Yes but I didn’t feel it. I mean being on a farm where you knew you had a roof and food on the table and all that, of course it was affected to a great degree but I really wasn’t aware of it.
Because you were a young — ten or twelve.
So after maybe reading later, you said well I lived through that.
Yeah. Well my wife was a bit younger, she doesn’t recall the depression, and we joked about that.
